title: Black Panther Party 60th Anniversary: Fred Hampton's Legacy Lives On in Chicago | Politics
text:
The Black Panther Party's 60th anniversary highlights Fred Hampton's enduring legacy in Chicago, where free breakfast programs and health clinics still inspire change.
Sixty years after the Black Panther Party was founded, its legacy continues to shape Chicago, particularly through the work of Fred Hampton and the Illinois chapter. The party, originally established in Oakland, California, in 1966 by Huey Newton and Bobby Seale, demanded change for the Black community. In Chicago, the Panthers' community health clinics and free breakfast programs redefined neighborhood care, and today a new generation is carrying forward that mission.
Founding and Early Impact
The Black Panther Party for Self-Defense was created in 1966 and became known for its armed patrols, black berets, and confrontational rhetoric against police brutality and racism. However, their legacy is also defined by their provision of food, water, and shelter for the Black community. In 1968, the movement established its Illinois chapter with 20-year-old Deputy Chairman Fred Hampton at the helm.
The Chicago Black Panthers' community health clinics and free breakfast programs helped redefine neighborhood care. What was once a radical act of feeding children before school is now reflected in school nutrition programs nationwide. Fred Hampton Jr., Chairman of the Black Panther Party Cubs, explained that the party's position was that anybody, regardless of color, could go to school hungry, and it is hard to even have a discussion or maintain attention when hungry.
They also helped build Chicago's Rainbow Coalition, uniting Black, Latino, and poor white communities around shared needs. This inspired a legacy carried on by organizations like Jesse Jackson's Rainbow PUSH.
Assassination of Fred Hampton
The Chicago Black Panther movement took a major hit in 1969. The FBI identified Hampton as a radical threat and teamed up with the Chicago Police to assassinate him. Hampton Jr. described it as a national hit, architected by FBI deputy director William Sullivan and created by FBI director J. Edgar Hoover. In Hoover's own words, the program was created to discredit, demise, disrupt, and destroy any Black nationalist movements, especially youth.
On December 4, 1969, Hampton was drugged, and police fired more than 100 shots into his home while he lay in bed with his pregnant wife. They also murdered Black Panther Mark Clark. Akua Njeri, Hampton Sr.'s widow, recalled that when the shooting started and she felt it going into the bed, she jumped on top of Chairman Fred to cover him, acting without thinking.
Former Congressman Bobby Rush said he was supposed to be in that house that day but ended up leaving. He recounted that as police were leaving, one officer said, well we killed Fred and Bobby Rush is next. Despite authorities denying any plot to assassinate Hampton Sr., survivors and relatives later filed a wrongful death lawsuit and settled for more than a million dollars.
Legacy and Ongoing Recognition
Hampton Jr. noted that J. Edgar Hoover said the Black Panther Party represented the number one internal threat, the internal political security system of the Civil War. Today, the Panther legacy lives on through Hampton Sr.'s son, Chairman Fred Hampton Jr., who now leads the Black Panther Party Cubs in Chicago, continuing his father's legacy.
The Hampton House in Maywood is now designated as a historical landmark. The Illinois Black Panther Party Heritage Trail is also documenting the people, places, and events that shaped the movement in Chicago, ensuring that the contributions of the Black Panther Party are remembered and its impact continues to inspire.
